title: Just finished watching Shutter Island (2010). -- short commentary

commenti.body: I watched Shutter Island in theaters when it came out. The moment he set foot from the ferry, I groaned inwardly because I saw the twist coming while the film hadn't even started yet. Normally, that wouldn't be much of an issue for me if the road to it was fascinating. Alas, I was bored most of the time. I read somewhere that Scorsese called it his least favorite film, and I can see why. I think he wanted a homage to Hitchcock, especially Vertigo with a hint of Cabinet of Dr. Caligari. The result was more like something from Mario Bava by the way of Argento. Personally, I felt the reflection on real-life atrocities like The Holocaust was misplaced. The setting felt far too campy to mix it up with those images.

This is the film Scorsese’s Cape Fear remake was trying to be. If you go into it with a modern eye I have a feeling you won’t like it. Shutter Island has a clear love affair with classic b-movies. If you go in with that mindset, it’s a great movie. Dare I say one of Scorsese’s best.

Sincerely, I like it. Watched at first at the movies and then at home. Second time was even better. It convinced me to read the book. The movie is better. Not every movie has to be a masterpiece; maybe SI is not a masterpiece and not the reason why you remember Scorsese, but it's still a very good thriller.

I saw it when it came out in a Manhattan theater and you would have thought it was a comedy based on audience response. I agree basically but moreso. It verges on the brink of parody but lacks humor. A total whiff.

Really surprised by the comments here. It’s a beloved movie. And plays with the thriller genre really well. It’s not actually a mystery to be solved be a meditation on guilt, grief, perception, violence, and consequence. There’s a ton of literary nuance going on. 

[Full deconstruction](https://filmcolossus.com/shutter-island-ending-explained)

I don’t think you have to love the film or anything. But I’d say it deserves a bit more respect then what some of the comments here are giving it.

I guess that means me. I respect most of Scorsese's work, but that doesn't mean I must respect everything he's made. Sorry, I think Shutter Island is a failure both as a thriller and as a meditation on guilt. As a film, I'd put it in the same category as Gangs of New York—great ambitions, but unsure of what it wants to be in the end.
How does it fail about meditating on guilt? Genuinely curious to hear your thoughts.

Well, how does it succeed? Sorry if that sounds like a cop-out. The key word for me is sincerity. Let me provide an example where Scorsese successfully reflects on the struggle of guilt and conflict: 'Silence.' 'Silence' doesn't rely on a gimmicky plot with false identities or red herrings and a shocking twist. Instead, we see the conflict of the main protagonist in his actions driving the plot forward. 'Shutter Island,' in comparison, left me with a bad taste in my mouth, but at no moment did I feel a conflict or guilt from the character, just an attempt at plot trickery.

I liked the movie, when I saw it in theaters back in the day, but I think there's an argument to be made that the middlebrow twist ending thriller was kind of played out by 2010. I think that might be part of the criticism.

Show Psycho to any GenZer and they can see the twist coming from a mile away. It's a still a mastpeiece. In fact I'd argue strongly that seeing the tiwst coming in Shutter Island is exceptionally besides the point, since many fans of this one seem to acknowledge that they saw it coming, but it succeeds in genre and dipicting the psychologocial inner. It even does the tired old trope of hidden messages being mixed up in an anagram and somehow it works. I personaly feel the reflections on real-life atrocities are some of the most profoundly arresting moments in all of cinema history. This is top tier Scorsese because he proves he can work in a genre that's not really his wheelhouse, and he does it again in Hugo.

I despise this movie. As you say, it's utterly empty. It's just a bunch of nonsense leading up to a ridiculous, mean-spirited, and idiotic surprise. It's supposedly about psychology, but nothing in the movie is connected on any way to real human behavior. There is no scenario where a psycologist would turn an island into a haunted-house for the benefit of a single patient. It would cost a million dollars even back then. The psychological conditions that the husband and wife suffer from are possibly real conditions I guess, but they are both sensational diseases that come straight out of the headlines, and the idea that these two 0.00001% of the population lunatics would get married is just dumb.

Dennis Lehane is the king of these idiotic surprise endings. His movies are clocks that work and snap into place with precision, but the individual gears are crazed, asymmetrical, and painted in ugly, mismatched patterns. These stories must appeal to people who want to see a bunch of sick characters who twist and abuse one another in hellish, insane, ways, but who also want a story with a neat, logical conclusion (like the end of an SVU episode... Those shows are also atrocious). Some of his other stories (Mystic River, Fine Baby Gone), at least, are good up until the arbitrarily byzantine endings, but Shutter Island is not good at any point (despite being very competently filmed, of course).
